narrative: The model estimated a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That does not mean failure is certain; it means the risk was judged higher than the school was prepared to accept, so your application was denied. The strongest signal against you was your Year 3 rank within your school: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. This was the most influential factor and pushed the prediction toward failure. Your Year 1 rank was the second most influential factor; you were in the second decile versus an accepted-student average near the sixth, and it also pushed toward failure, though less strongly. Your undergraduate GPA was the third most influential factor. At 2.50 it is below the accepted-student average of about 3.23, but in this prediction it was the one top factor that nudged the estimate toward passing rather than failure. To improve a future application, seek specific admissions feedback, strengthen your academic record through additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program, retake the LSAT if it can be improved, and build a concrete bar-exam preparation plan. Reapply only after you can show evidence of stronger academic readiness and explain how your later performance better predicts success.
